front: Which annotation configures how a JPA entity's primary key value is generated?
back: @GeneratedValue
accepted_answers: @GeneratedValue
hint: It is commonly paired with a strategy such as IDENTITY or SEQUENCE.

front: Which JPA annotation marks a field that should not be persisted to the database?
back: @Transient
accepted_answers: @Transient
hint: The field still exists on the Java object but Hibernate ignores it for mapping.

front: Which annotation declares a one-to-many relationship from the parent entity to a collection of child entities?
back: @OneToMany
accepted_answers: @OneToMany
hint: It is often paired with mappedBy on the owning child side.

front: What is the difference between FetchType.LAZY and FetchType.EAGER?
back: LAZY defers loading an association until it is first accessed, while EAGER loads the association immediately together with the owning entity, which can pull in far more data than a given use case needs.
accepted_answers: LAZY defers loading until accessed; EAGER loads immediately with the owner
hint: LAZY is generally the safer default for associations that are not always needed.

front: What is the difference between the first-level persistence context cache and a second-level cache in Hibernate?
back: The first-level cache is scoped to a single EntityManager or session and is always on, while the second-level cache is optional, shared across sessions, and configured per entity or region to reduce repeated database hits across transactions.
accepted_answers: first-level cache is per-session and always on; second-level cache is optional and shared across sessions
hint: The first-level cache disappears when the persistence context closes.

front: Why does the owning side of a bidirectional @OneToMany and @ManyToOne relationship matter for which side controls the foreign key?
back: Only the owning side's changes are written to the foreign key column; the inverse side marked with mappedBy is not itself persisted, so updating only the inverse side's collection without updating the owning side leaves the database foreign key unchanged.
accepted_answers: only the owning side's changes update the foreign key; the mappedBy side is not persisted directly
hint: The side without mappedBy is almost always the owning side.

front: What is the difference between CascadeType.PERSIST and CascadeType.REMOVE on a parent-to-child association?
back: CascadeType.PERSIST propagates saving the parent to also save any new, unsaved child entities, while CascadeType.REMOVE propagates deleting the parent to also delete its associated children, and each must be chosen deliberately based on whether children can exist independently.
accepted_answers: PERSIST cascades saving children; REMOVE cascades deleting children
hint: Cascading REMOVE is dangerous for children that other entities might also reference.

front: Why does calling a setter on a managed entity inside a transaction not require an explicit repository save() call to persist the change?
back: Hibernate tracks a managed entity through dirty checking, so any field change detected on a managed instance within the transaction is automatically included in the UPDATE issued at flush or commit, without needing an explicit save call.
accepted_answers: dirty checking automatically detects changes on managed entities and flushes them without an explicit save
hint: This only applies to entities that are currently managed or attached, not detached ones.

front: A @OneToMany collection declared FetchType.LAZY is accessed for the first time after the enclosing EntityManager or session has already closed. What is thrown?
back: LazyInitializationException, because Hibernate can only load a lazy association while the owning entity is still attached to an open persistence context.
accepted_answers: LazyInitializationException because the persistence context is already closed
hint: This is one of the most common causes of a service-layer exception thrown from a view or serialization layer.

front: save() is called for two separate new entity instances that both have the identical value in a column with a unique database constraint, with no application-level check. What happens on the second save at flush time?
back: A DataIntegrityViolationException, wrapping a database unique constraint violation, is thrown when the second insert conflicts with the already-flushed unique value.
accepted_answers: a DataIntegrityViolationException from the unique constraint violation
hint: The database enforces uniqueness even when the application layer does not check first.

front: An entity has @Id @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.IDENTITY), and code calls save() inside a loop for a batch of 1000 rows. What limitation does the IDENTITY strategy impose on Hibernate's batching?
back: IDENTITY requires the database to generate the key at insert time, so Hibernate cannot know the id ahead of time and must execute each insert individually, disabling JDBC batch inserts for that entity.
accepted_answers: IDENTITY disables JDBC batch inserts since Hibernate must insert one row at a time to get each generated key
hint: SEQUENCE-based generation can be pre-allocated and batched more efficiently.

front: merge() is called on a detached entity whose id does not match any row currently in the database. What happens?
back: Hibernate treats it as a request to persist a new row for that id, since merge copies the detached entity's state onto a managed instance matched by id and inserts one if no matching row exists.
accepted_answers: Hibernate inserts a new row for that id since no managed entity with that id currently exists
hint: merge always returns a different, managed instance rather than mutating the detached one you passed in.

front: A REST endpoint that serializes an entity directly to JSON throws a stack overflow whenever the entity has a bidirectional @OneToMany and @ManyToOne relationship. What is the cause and fix?
back: Serializing both sides of a bidirectional relationship directly causes the child to serialize its parent, which serializes its children again, recursing indefinitely; the fix is to serialize a DTO that only exposes one direction, or mark one side with @JsonIgnore or the managed and back reference annotations.
accepted_answers: infinite recursion from serializing both sides of the bidirectional relationship; fix with a DTO or Jackson reference annotations
hint: The cycle exists because parent and child each hold a reference back to the other.

front: A service method updates several entities in a loop with no explicit transaction boundary, and only some of the updates are visible after an error partway through. What is missing?
back: The method is missing a transaction boundary such as @Transactional around the whole unit of work, so without one each save can commit independently and a failure partway through leaves the database in a partially updated, inconsistent state.
accepted_answers: missing an explicit transaction boundary so partial failures leave inconsistent partial updates
hint: All-or-nothing behavior requires the operations to share one transaction.

front: A repository method loads 1000 parent entities and then accesses a LAZY child collection on each one, producing 1001 separate SQL SELECT statements in the logs. What problem is this and what is one fix?
back: This is the N+1 select problem; a fix is to use a JOIN FETCH in the query, an entity graph, or batch fetching, so the children are loaded together with the parents in a small, fixed number of queries.
accepted_answers: the N+1 select problem; fix with JOIN FETCH, an entity graph, or batch fetching
hint: Count how many SQL statements a single logical operation produces.

front: An entity field is annotated @Column(nullable = false) and validated correctly in Java, but inserting a row with a null value still succeeds at the database level. What is the likely gap?
back: nullable = false mainly affects DDL generation, so if the actual database column allows NULL, for example because the schema was created separately or a migration did not add the constraint, Hibernate's annotation alone does not enforce it at write time.
accepted_answers: nullable=false mainly affects generated DDL, not an already-existing column without the constraint
hint: The database schema is the actual source of truth for a NOT NULL constraint, not the annotation by itself.

front: Updating an entity fetched in one transaction and saving it in a second, later transaction throws OptimisticLockException. What feature caused this and why?
back: The entity has a @Version field for optimistic locking; another transaction updated and incremented the version between the read and the write, so Hibernate detects the version mismatch and rejects the stale update instead of silently overwriting newer data.
accepted_answers: a @Version field caused optimistic locking to detect a stale write and reject it
hint: Optimistic locking trades an occasional retry for avoiding silent lost updates.

back: SELECT o FROM Order o WHERE o.customer.id = :customerId ORDER BY o.orderDate DESC
accepted_answers: SELECT o FROM Order o WHERE o.customer.id = :customerId ORDER BY o.orderDate DESC
hint: JPQL queries entity names and fields, not table and column names.

front: Write a Spring Data JPA repository method declaration that finds all Order entities with a status field equal to a given OrderStatus, using query derivation from the method name.
back: List<Order> findByStatus(OrderStatus status);
accepted_answers: List<Order> findByStatus(OrderStatus status);
hint: Spring Data derives the query from the method name's findBy property pattern.

front: Write a JOIN FETCH JPQL query that loads a Customer entity together with its orders collection in one query, given a customerId.
back: SELECT c FROM Customer c JOIN FETCH c.orders WHERE c.id = :customerId
accepted_answers: SELECT c FROM Customer c JOIN FETCH c.orders WHERE c.id = :customerId
hint: JOIN FETCH avoids a separate lazy-load query for the orders collection.
